title: Given a scenario, perform OS installations and upgrades in a diverse OS environment

subtopics.heading: Linux overview
subtopics.notes:
Linux is a free, open-source OS derived from Unix. Runs on a wide range of hardware from modern servers to older machines. Multiple distributions (distros): Ubuntu, Debian, Red Hat, and many others. Commands are consistent across all distros.

Community-supported - no single vendor. This means driver support for very new hardware may lag.

Boot process:
1. UEFI firmware reads the EFI System Partition (ESP) on the boot drive.
2. ESP contains .efi bootloader files - one per OS.
3. Bootloader starts the OS kernel.
4. Kernel loads device drivers, manages hardware and processes.
5. Kernel starts systemd.
6. systemd starts all background daemons (services).

Kernel vs user space:
- Kernel space: protected memory area where the kernel runs.
- User space: where all other applications run.

systemd - modern Linux service manager. Starts/stops/manages daemons. Replaced older init systems to provide one consistent toolset.

root user - the Linux superuser. Equivalent to Windows Administrator. All system changes require root or sudo.

macOS and Linux share many commands because macOS is derived from BSD Unix.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Boot sequence: UEFI ESP > bootloader > kernel > systemd > daemons. root = Linux admin. systemd manages daemons.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing daemons (Linux background services) with Windows services. They are functionally equivalent but the terminology differs.

subtopics.heading: Key Linux configuration files
subtopics.notes:
All in /etc directory:

/etc/passwd - user account database. One line per user. Fields: username:x:UID:GID:comment:home_dir:shell. The x means hashed password is in shadow file.

/etc/shadow - protected file containing hashed passwords. Not readable by regular users. Contains: username, password hash, last-changed date, expiration data. Protects against brute force of hashes.

/etc/hosts - static hostname-to-IP mapping. Checked BEFORE DNS. Overrides DNS for any listed entry. Pre-DNS origin; still useful for local overrides.

/etc/resolv.conf - lists DNS servers the system uses for name resolution. Check this to confirm DNS configuration.

/etc/fstab - File System Table. Lists all drives and partitions that mount at boot, their mount points, and file system types. If a drive is missing after boot, check fstab.
subtopics.whyOnExam: /etc/hosts overrides DNS. /etc/shadow has the actual password hashes and is restricted. /etc/resolv.conf = DNS server config. /etc/fstab = what mounts at boot.
subtopics.commonTrap: Thinking /etc/passwd still contains passwords. It shows 'x' in the password field; the actual hashes are in /etc/shadow.

subtopics.heading: Linux file system commands
subtopics.notes:
Navigation:
- ls - list directory contents. ls -la shows permissions, ownership, size for all files.
- cd - change directory. cd ~ or bare cd returns to home directory.
- pwd - print working directory (show current path).
- mv source dest - move or rename a file. No separate rename command.
- cp source dest - copy a file.
- rm filename - delete a file. rm -r directory - delete directory and its contents.
- find . -name "third*" - find files by name. Supports wildcards.
- cat file - display file contents. cat f1 f2 > out - concatenate and redirect.
- man command - show manual page for any command. Q to quit.

Permissions (chmod):
- Three groups: user (u), group (g), others (o).
- Three permissions: read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1).
- Octal notation: chmod 744 file → user=rwx(7), group=r(4), others=r(4).
- Letter notation: chmod u+x file (add execute for user), chmod a-w file (remove write for all).
- View permissions: ls -l. First column shows type + 9 permission bits (e.g. -rwxr--r--).

Ownership (chown):
- chown user file - change file owner.
- chown user:group file - change owner and group.
- Requires elevated privileges (use sudo).

Elevation:
- sudo command - run one command with superuser privileges.
- su - switch the entire terminal session to superuser. Use exit to return.
- Best practice: use sudo rather than su for individual commands.

File system check and mounting:
- fsck - file system check utility (like Windows chkdsk). Runs at boot; checks for logical errors.
- mount - view or mount file systems. Bare mount lists all current mount points.
- mount is similar to Windows net use but more integrated into the OS.
subtopics.whyOnExam: chmod octal values: 7=rwx, 6=rw-, 5=r-x, 4=r--. sudo vs su. mv = rename. ls -la = full listing with permissions.
subtopics.commonTrap: Thinking rm deletes directories. rm alone only deletes files. Use rm -r to delete a directory and its contents.

subtopics.heading: Linux network and search commands
subtopics.notes:
ip address - show IP configuration for all adapters (equivalent to Windows ipconfig /all). Shows IP, subnet, broadcast, MAC, IPv6.
ip route - show the routing table.

ping - test ICMP reachability. Linux ping runs continuously until stopped with Ctrl+C. Windows ping stops after 4 packets by default.

curl - retrieve content from a URL: curl http://example.com. Returns raw HTML. Used for scripting and testing web servers from the command line.

dig - DNS query tool. Equivalent to Windows nslookup but with more detailed output. Shows query, answer section with resolved IPs.

traceroute - maps the hop-by-hop path to a destination. Windows equivalent: tracert. Uses TTL-exceeded messages. Some hops may show * if the router filters ICMP.

grep "text" filename - search file contents for a string. Works on single or multiple files. Output: every matching line.

Package managers (install/remove applications):
- apt (Ubuntu/Debian): sudo apt install packagename
- dnf (Red Hat/Fedora): successor to YUM. Use if apt is unavailable.
subtopics.whyOnExam: Linux ping runs until Ctrl+C. dig = Linux DNS query (nslookup equivalent). traceroute = Linux path tracer (tracert equivalent). apt for Debian-based distros, dnf for Red Hat.
subtopics.commonTrap: Running ping on Linux and waiting for it to stop. Unlike Windows (4 packets), Linux ping runs indefinitely.

subtopics.heading: Linux process and disk commands
subtopics.notes:
top - real-time process monitor. Shows all processes with CPU, memory usage. Updates every second. Windows equivalent: Task Manager. Load average shown as 3 numbers: 1-min, 5-min, 15-min averages.

ps - list processes (snapshot, not real-time).
- ps - current user's processes only.
- ps -e - all processes on the system.
- ps -e | grep term - filter to find specific processes.

df -h - disk free. Shows mounted file systems with used/available space. -h = human-readable (GB/MB). Windows equivalent: looking at drive properties.

du -h - disk usage. Shows space consumed by each directory and subdirectory. Use to find what is filling a disk.

nano - full-screen text editor. Opens in terminal. Used to edit config files. Ctrl+X to exit (prompts to save).

systemd and daemons:
- Linux background services = daemons.
- systemd manages all daemons: start, stop, enable at boot.
- Commands: systemctl start/stop/enable/disable <service>
subtopics.whyOnExam: top = Linux Task Manager. df -h = disk free. du -h = disk usage (find what is filling disk). ps -e = all processes. nano = text editor.
subtopics.commonTrap: Confusing df (how much space is FREE on each filesystem) with du (how much space is USED by directories). They answer different questions.
